key_insight: The paper characterizes when the mean of a Gaussian can be identified from coarse (partitioned) observations and gives polynomial-time estimators that achieve near-optimal sample complexity and provable error rates.
problem_solved: How to estimate the mean of a d-dimensional Gaussian when each sample is observed only as the cell of a partition that contains it (e.g., rounding, sensor bins, censoring), resolving identifiability, statistical limits, and computational tractability for coarse data.
method: Characterize identifiability and minimax/sample-complexity tradeoffs for Gaussian mean estimation under general partition/coarsening schemes.
Design computationally efficient estimators (convex/likelihood-based relaxations and spectral/moment-based methods) with provable error bounds matching information-theoretic limits in key regimes.
Prove matching lower bounds showing which partition structures make estimation fundamentally hard and quantify how coarsening degrades rates.
impact: Provides practitioners principled tools and guarantees for mean estimation from quantized, rounded, or censored measurements—useful for low-bandwidth sensors, privacy-preserving releases, and econometric lagged/aggregated data. It also guides partition design and sample-size planning when working with coarse observations.
visual_elements: Schematic: true Gaussian samples mapped to partition cells (points → colored bins) to illustrate coarse observation model.
Line chart: estimation error versus sample size comparing full-data estimator and proposed coarse-data algorithms (showing near-optimal scaling).
Flowchart: algorithmic pipeline (data → estimator choice: convex/spectral → output) with complexity and guarantee callouts.
Heatmap/table: regions of identifiability and sample-complexity as a function of partition granularity and dimensionality.
paper_title: Mean Estimation from Coarse Data: Characterizations and Efficient Algorithms
paper_authors: Alkis Kalavasis, Anay Mehrotra, Manolis Zampetakis, Felix Zhou, Ziyu Zhu
